summary: Provides an applicability statement for the VPN solution described in RFC 4364 and related documents. It helps readers judge where that approach fits. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: A guide that tells you when a certain private-network tool is a good choice and when it is not.

questions: what is a bgp mpls vpn
when should i use a bgp mpls vpn
subtitle: When BGP/MPLS IP VPNs are the right tool, and how they handle isolation, addressing, scale and management.

tldr.problem: Customers and providers need to judge whether the BGP/MPLS IP VPN solution of RFC 4364 fits their situation, measured against the L3VPN requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The applicability statement goes through provisioning, topologies, isolation, security, addressing, access, routing, migration, scalability, QoS and management, saying what the scheme does and does not provide.
tldr.outcome: It suits customers who want the provider to run their inter-site routing, and it says it is not the answer for customers who want to build their own overlay of secure tunnels across the Internet.

today: RFC 4365 is an Informational applicability statement from February 2006 for the solution in RFC 4364. According to the metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Who Is This VPN For
sections.content:
This document is an applicability statement for the VPN solution in RFC 4364, called BGP/MPLS IP VPNs because BGP distributes the routes and MPLS makes packets follow particular routes. A service provider (SP) offers it to a customer.

The target customer carries only IP packets, does not want to manage a routed backbone, and wants the backbone to be transparent to its own routing. Its routers need to know only the Provider Edge (PE) routers its sites attach to. The target SP has an IP backbone with MPLS-enabled edge routers and does not want a distinct overlay of tunnels per customer. The basic idea is to model each VPN as a self-contained internet, where the SP strictly controls route distribution so that VPN routes do not leave the VPN unless the customer authorizes it.

It is explicitly not the right solution for customers who want to join sites over the public Internet by buying the cheapest local connectivity. They need an overlay of secure tunnels. Customers who want full control of backbone routing may prefer a virtual router service.
sections.eli5: It is for a company that wants the phone company to carry all its messages between offices and hide how. A company that wants to run the roads itself should pick something else.

sections.title: How the Provider Sets It Up
sections.content:
For each VPN attached to a PE router, the SP configures a VPN Routing and Forwarding table (VRF) and associates each local access link with it. The PE learns routes from attached CE routers using EBGP, RIP, OSPF or static routing. If an IGP runs on the access links it MUST be a separate instance from the backbone IGP and from other VPNs' instances. Each PE runs BGP and peers with a small set of Route Reflectors. A full mesh of IBGP would not scale to large networks.

Each VRF is configured with three things. A Route Distinguisher (RD) is a globally unique 8-byte value prepended to IPv4 prefixes to form the VPN-IPv4 address family, so overlapping address spaces stay unique. One or more export Route Targets (RTs) are carried by BGP with routes leaving the VRF. One or more import RTs choose which routes to bring in. In the simplest case the RD and RTs are identical and all VRFs of a VPN exchange routes, as in an intranet. Setting them differently gives finer control and enables extranets. RTs must always be configured, but an RD can be assigned automatically.

Adding a site means attaching its CE to a PE, configuring the interface and associating it with the VRF. Changes are propagated to other PEs by BGP.
sections.eli5: Each customer gets its own private address book in the provider's router. Labels on routes decide which address books may copy from which, so one customer never sees another's entries.

sections.title: Topologies, Traffic and Isolation
sections.content:
The scheme is optimized for full connectivity between sites, yet Route Targets let the SP build hub-and-spoke, partial mesh or paths that force traffic through a third site, even down to a single route. Unicast IP is fully supported. Multicast is optional and needs the mechanisms of a separate document, with scaling implications. Non-IP traffic is not supported, so the customer would need an SP layer 2 service or IP tunnels.

VPN routes are a different BGP address family from ordinary Internet routes. They are not leaked to the Internet, and Internet routes are not leaked in, unless a VRF is explicitly configured that way, and that is not the default. Two VPNs on the same PE have strict separation of forwarding and routing. Traffic between sites is encapsulated across the backbone. The RFC compares this isolation to classical Frame Relay or ATM L2 VPNs: the customer relies on the SP to configure the backbone correctly.
sections.eli5: The provider can choose which offices can talk to which, in a full web, a star or something odd. Private mail stays private and does not leak out to the open Internet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No particular means of protecting user data is specified. Optional PE-to-PE IPsec procedures can authenticate or encrypt data between ingress and egress PE, though data is exposed at those PEs and on the access links. Customers can run their own IPsec, which is transparent to the scheme as long as a cleartext IP header reaches the PE.

The SP must keep illegitimate traffic out of VPNs. PE and P routers must be secure, LDP and BGP sessions between them should be authenticated (TCP MD5 or IPsec), and MPLS packets from external interfaces should not be accepted unless the top label was legitimately distributed. Where IP encapsulation is used, packets addressed to PE routers should be filtered at the border. If the public Internet carries the VPN backbone, IPsec tunnels should always be used.

A dynamic routing protocol on the CE-PE link can overload a PE with updates, a possible denial-of-service attack. Mitigations include resource partitioning per VPN, rate limits and shutting the interface. The RFC also answers a PPVPN security-framework template question by question. It says the approach gives complete address and route separation, but the scheme cannot by itself prevent or detect misconfiguration, which it treats as network management. An optional CE verification procedure can detect a wrongly connected site.
sections.eli5: The provider has to lock its own equipment and check who is connecting. Guests who want their messages secret from everyone, even the provider, should add their own locks.

sections.title: Addressing, Access and Routing
sections.content:
Overlapping customer addresses are supported and need not follow RFC 1918, though the addresses reachable from a given site must be unique. NAT at the VPN edge is transparent to the scheme. IPv6 is not precluded, provided PE/CE routing supports it and PE-PE BGP supports the labeled IPv6 address family, which the RFC says is not yet specified but is obvious from the IPv4 one. Layer 2 addresses are never carried across the backbone.

Access can be physical or logical with no link-layer restriction. Dial-up PPP users can be assigned to a VRF using the SP's AAA server and then authenticated again by the customer's. IPsec access is possible too. A CE may be homed to two or more PEs. Internet and VPN access can share an interface by importing Internet routes into the VRF, and the route to the Internet can lead to a firewall at another site. Backbone routing is independent of VPNs: VPN routes travel PE to Route Reflector to PE and are never seen by P routers. Direct PE-PE interworking with other VPN solutions is not supported.
sections.eli5: Two customers may use the same house numbers and nothing gets mixed up. Offices can connect in several ways, and the customer may keep a separate door to the public Internet.

sections.title: Scalability, QoS and Management
sections.content:
The RFC says there is no upper limit on the number of VPNs per SP network, because no one box needs to know every VPN. Only PEs attached to a VPN and the Route Reflectors that carry its routes hold state for it, and P routers keep no per-VPN state. The main constraint is how many routes a given PE can support. The SP may need significant planning, for instance rehoming sites to different PEs. Inter-AS option (a) does not scale well, and option (c) saves border routers from holding VPN routes at the cost of every AS needing a route to the PEs in the others. VPN multicast trade-offs are described as not yet well understood.

QoS items such as policing, shaping, traffic engineering and DSCP mapping are not VPN-specific, and depend on edge and core platform features. The scheme supports the hose model naturally and the pipe model through traffic engineering. The SP manages PE devices, for example with the MIBs the RFC lists, and is not required to manage CEs. CE devices hold no VPN-specific information. For migration, sites are moved one at a time and VPN-backbone routes are preferred over the legacy backbone, usually by adjusting IGP metrics.
sections.eli5: No single machine has to know about every customer, so the system can keep growing. The real limit is how many routes one edge router can remember.

items.title: Route Distinguisher
items.text: Globally unique 8-byte value prepended to IPv4 prefixes, forming VPN-IPv4 addresses.

items.title: Export Route Target
items.text: Carried by BGP with routes leaving the VRF.

items.title: Import Route Target
items.text: Selects which routes are imported into the VRF.
